opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's one of the most remarkable things about human cognition, and it's something we take completely for granted. Think about what you actually do in a single day. You might decide, at a very high level, that you want to finish a research paper, or get a PhD, or go to a conference in another country. And that abstract goal eventually turns into millions of individual motor commands: moving your fingers on a keyboard, shifting your weight as you walk, the muscle activations involved in speaking. Something like a trillion of those primitive actions over a lifetime. And yet we never plan at that level. Nobody plans a trip to Paris by thinking about which muscle to contract next.

What we do instead is work with this enormous library of abstract actions at many levels of granularity. "Go to Paris" breaks down into "get to the airport," "fly," "get to the hotel." "Get to the airport" breaks down into "call a taxi" or "take the train," and so on, down to things that are essentially reflexes. The power comes from the fact that at each level you can reason about consequences without filling in all the details. I can be pretty confident that if I book a flight and show up at the airport, I'll get to Paris, without having worked out how I'll get from the gate to the plane. That lets you look ahead over very long time horizons, years in some cases, which would be completely impossible if you were searching over primitive actions.

And the other side of it is that we commit only partially. You have a high-level plan, you start executing the first bits, and you refine the rest as you go, when you actually have the information you need. That's enormously efficient, and it's robust, because the world doesn't cooperate with detailed plans made far in advance.

The reason I emphasize this is that it's one of the places where I think AI systems are still quite far from what humans do. We've built systems that are very good at fixed-horizon problems, like Go, where the action space is given to you. But the real world requires you to discover and construct these abstract actions yourself, and to know which abstractions are reliable, what they achieve, when they apply. We do that so naturally that we hardly notice it. Getting machines to build and use those hierarchies across their whole lifetime of activity is, I think, one of the big open problems on the way to general-purpose intelligence. And frankly, it's also one of the reasons I think we should be careful about predictions that it's just a matter of scaling up what we have now.

r001.rationale: The response describes abstract goals being carried through a hierarchy down to primitive motor commands, and says people do this naturally without planning at the primitive level.

r002.rationale: It explains that abstract reasoning lets people assess consequences without filling in low-level details and plan over long horizons, which would be infeasible over primitive actions.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, think about what you did this morning. You decided to come here, and that decision was made at a level of abstraction that didn't involve any muscle commands at all. It was something like, "I'll go to the studio." Then that got refined into "I'll take the Tube," and then into "walk to the station," and eventually, when it mattered, into actually moving your legs and avoiding the person coming the other way on the pavement. You never, at any point, planned the whole thing as a sequence of motor-control actions. If you tried to, you'd never leave the house. A human lifetime, in terms of primitive motor actions, is something like twenty trillion steps, and it's simply not feasible to do lookahead search over that space.

So what we do, and what I think is one of the central tricks of human intelligence, is to construct a hierarchy of abstract actions, and to reason at whichever level is appropriate. At the high level you commit to things like "finish the PhD" or "visit my parents next month," and those commitments constrain what happens below them without specifying it. Then you defer the details until the information needed to fill them in actually becomes available. You don't decide which foot you'll put on the escalator first until you're standing in front of it, because there's no point.

What's remarkable is that this is all learned and shared culturally. Nobody is born knowing the action "book a flight." We acquire this enormous library of abstract actions from other people, which means every individual benefits from the accumulated discovery of what works as a useful unit of behavior. And when you have that library, planning becomes almost trivial. A plan at the top level might have three or four steps, and each of those is something you already know how to do.

The reason I find this so important for AI is that our systems still mostly don't do it. Reinforcement learning agents, even the impressive ones, are largely planning or acting at a single very fine temporal grain, and they get away with it only because the environments are small. If you want something that operates over days, months, or years in the real world, it has to have this capability of managing commitments across levels of abstraction. We've shown mathematically that you can do this correctly, that you can have a hierarchical planner that makes high-level decisions with guarantees that there's a way to carry them out, but the piece we really don't understand yet is where the hierarchy itself comes from. How does a system discover that "make a cup of tea" is a worthwhile thing to have a name for? That's the question that, to me, sits right at the heart of getting to general-purpose intelligence.

r001.rationale: The response describes human intelligence as using a hierarchy of abstract actions, reasoning at the appropriate level, and refining plans into lower-level actions when needed.

r002.rationale: It explains that high-level planning avoids infeasible search over primitive motor actions and makes planning tractable, with short plans built from familiar actions.

astra-6.text:
Well, think about planning a trip. You might say, “I’m going to Paris,” and then work out how to get to the airport, and then how to get a taxi. You don’t begin by planning every muscle movement needed to pick up your suitcase. You can reason about the trip at one level and fill in the details at another when you need them.

That’s enormously powerful because the number of low-level actions involved in any substantial activity is huge. If you had to consider all of them at once, you’d never get anywhere. Abstraction lets you set aside most of those details while preserving what matters for the decision you’re making.

And we can move between levels. If the taxi doesn’t arrive, we reconsider how to get to the airport; we don’t necessarily reconsider the whole purpose of the trip. That ability to organize behavior over many different timescales is a major part of what makes human intelligence effective.

r001.rationale: The response describes reasoning about a trip at one level, filling in lower-level actions as needed, and shifting levels when plans change to organize behavior across different timescales.

r002.rationale: It explains that abstraction lets people ignore low-level details while preserving what matters for a decision, avoiding an otherwise overwhelming amount of reasoning.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, think about planning a trip. You might say, “I’m going to Paris,” and reason about why you want to go, when you’ll go, and what you’ll do there. You don’t have to think about every muscle movement involved in getting out of your chair, packing a suitcase, or reaching the airport. Those details can be filled in when they become relevant.

That’s an extraordinary ability, because a real-world activity might involve millions of little actions. If we had to reason through all of them at once, we’d never get anywhere. Abstraction lets us make decisions over long stretches of time while keeping the reasoning manageable.

And we can move between levels. If somebody tells you the airport is closed, you reconsider part of the plan. If your suitcase won’t close, you solve that much more local problem. We do this constantly, almost without noticing. Building AI systems that can choose useful abstractions and move between them as flexibly as we do is a very important challenge.

r001.rationale: It describes planning at a high level while filling in action details when relevant, then shifting to local problems as circumstances change—an everyday, largely unnoticed coordination across abstraction levels.

r002.rationale: It says abstraction keeps reasoning manageable and supports decisions over long stretches, but does not clearly explain that higher-level reasoning enables computations with exceptionally high decision-making value.
